They own the AFAS match rules, tolerances, VAT-code mappings and the supplier master data (IBAN, KvK, g-rekening). Within limits the Controller sets, they decide which suppliers and invoice types may post without anyone touching them. The job becomes more expert: less typing, more judgement on exceptions, tax treatment and data quality.

They gain the right to set match tolerances, send a bad supplier file back, hold one invoice out of a Rabobank batch, refuse an unconfirmed IBAN, and flag a small-supplier term past 30 days. Agency cost is split by site in the week it is worked, small carriers are paid inside 30 days, and FP&A gets a cash list before the nightly dashboard. The month closes faster because the invoices that match are already posted, and the adjustments that remain are named. The role stays, because someone still has to decide the breaks the forecast depends on.

In a normal month the three bookkeepers work exception queues for three sites. Invoices and bank lines that match post under rules the controller has agreed. Each morning the credit officer sees unmatched cash. Tilburg and Venlo get the same creditor, debtor and consumable-cost pack as Rotterdam, and a working-day-2 list of what is still open. Each quarter the finance director has a file per agency showing the wage tax and VAT went to the g-rekening. Days to close then depend on real exceptions and on other teams' accruals. The forecast starts from actuals the sites recognise. The desk is more expert on those exceptions and smaller as a keying operation.

They measure touchless processing, unresolved-item age, days sales outstanding and their contribution to close time, while the Controller and FP&A Analyst use cleaner inputs for a forecast the business trusts. ceiling_note.text: The ceiling is judgment, dual control and the documents that still arrive as PDF, not keying speed. Recording is about 103 hours a year per FTE and can shrink; close week, peak-season flex (up to 300 workers) and supplier disputes set the floor. Three people cannot also become the Controller or the credit function. This role does not take the absence file under the Wet verbetering poortwachter. The works council has a say if a match on agency hours starts following named flex workers. Under the EU AI Act this stays a low-stakes document and ledger process only while it does not score workers or make a credit decision about a person.

Three people at a loaded €45 an hour, each of these tasks only about 40 to 60 hours a year, so typing speed is not the limit. The limit is exception volume in close week and in the flex peak, plus gates that stay with a person: payment approval, the VAT return, the g-rekening, the 30-day rule for small suppliers, and the payroll specialist's sign-off on wages. Hours, receipts and rates that never enter AFAS cannot be fixed from the finance desk. The works council and AVG limit how far pay and expense data can be opened.

Most of these tasks are small (20–40 hours per FTE a year); the big gains sit in invoice processing and bank matching. Limits are messy PDF and agency invoices, own VAT codes per administration, and that the Controller and Finance Director keep sign-off on returns and the trial balance.

The seven supplied tasks total 215.6 hours per FTE annually, about 13.5% of a 1,600-hour role; savings here cannot be extrapolated to the whole job. The estimates are incremental planning assumptions that include remaining review, exception handling and recurring upkeep, but exclude initial implementation. Existing AFAS and Power BI automation, unavailable site data, physical investigations and specialist approvals limit the opportunity; the inferred current workflows need validation.

These eight tasks cover about 412 hours per FTE annually, roughly 26% of the supplied role-time baseline. The task estimates imply about 166 hours saved per FTE annually before allowing for overlap, shared reviews and ongoing maintenance; they are planning assumptions, not measured savings or a headcount reduction. Existing AFAS automation, missing operational sources, approval separation and disputed transactions limit further gains.

Each FTE has about 1,600 hours a year. The eight tasks here cover about 31% of them (about 500 hours per FTE). The approval gates stay manual, and so do PDF suppliers, agency invoices and anything that needs a phone call. The top teams in APQC's benchmark handle more than 20,000 invoices per FTE a year, so the limit is how many exceptions come in and how clean the supplier data is, not hours spent keying. Payment approval and posting rights stay with people under the four-eyes principle and the auditor's expectations.

These seven tasks are about 13.5% of the role, roughly 216 hours a year per person. The rest of the job, invoice capture, payment runs and customer billing, still sets the week. Three people cannot also be FP&A, credit control and payroll. Separation of duties caps it: the same person cannot change a supplier IBAN, approve the payment and clear the bank line, or count stock and approve the write-off. Close still waits on other teams' accruals and on the sites sending documents late. A personal productivity score of the three bookkeepers would be a works-council matter, so the logs cover transactions and not a scoreboard.
